power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified.

We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses.
SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h² = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected.

Gene-set analyses implicated gammaaminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (SLC17A6) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses.
Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal.
A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR=1.05, 95% CI 1.02-1.08, p=0.002).

Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS.
In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response.
Selfreported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission.
Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response.
Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is among the most prevalent and disabling conditions globally (1).
text.formatted: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is among the most prevalent and disabling conditions globally <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a first-line pharmacological treatment (2) and the most widely prescribed antidepressant class (3), yet response is highly variable.
Clinician-rated remission over 6-12-week trials occurs in around one-third of individuals (4), whereas up to 75% self-report benefit (5).
text.formatted: Clinician-rated remission over 6-12-week trials occurs in around one-third of individuals (4), whereas up to 75% self-report benefit <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: This gap may reflect differences in outcome definition (remission versus perceived benefit), trial duration, recall bias, or how clinicians and patients judge meaningful improvement, and understanding it may provide insight into the biological mechanisms underlying SSRI response.
Genetic variation contributes to differences in antidepressant treatment outcomes (6) (7) (8) (9), with single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability estimated at 13% (7).
text.formatted: Genetic variation contributes to differences in antidepressant treatment outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>, with single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability estimated at 13% <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: As with many traits in psychiatry, antidepressant treatment response is highly polygenic (6) (7) (8) 10), and genetic liability to other psychiatric disorders has been associated with poorer outcomes (11).
text.formatted: As with many traits in psychiatry, antidepressant treatment response is highly polygenic <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref>, and genetic liability to other psychiatric disorders has been associated with poorer outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: To date, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have found no robustly replicated loci.

A recent fivecohort meta-analysis of SSRI response identified a single novel locus by combining electronic health record-based, self-reported and clinical trial response phenotypes, but combining phenotypes trades larger samples against greater heterogeneity (8).
text.formatted: A recent fivecohort meta-analysis of SSRI response identified a single novel locus by combining electronic health record-based, self-reported and clinical trial response phenotypes, but combining phenotypes trades larger samples against greater heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Self-reported response mitigates this trade-off.
A comparable self-report question across studies provides consistent ascertainment at larger sample sizes than clinical phenotypes allow.
Collected via large-scale questionnaires, self-report is patient-centered and scalable, and may capture aspects of treatment outcome not routinely recorded in clinical settings (5).
text.formatted: Collected via large-scale questionnaires, self-report is patient-centered and scalable, and may capture aspects of treatment outcome not routinely recorded in clinical settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Despite recall bias, the resulting sample size gains may increase power for locus discovery and improve genetic architecture estimates. .

One explanation for the disparity between clinically assessed and self-reported response is that self-report captures improvement over longer periods than trials, as real-world antidepressant use often extends over several years (12).
text.formatted: One explanation for the disparity between clinically assessed and self-reported response is that self-report captures improvement over longer periods than trials, as real-world antidepressant use often extends over several years <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: If so, genetic and transcriptomic signals for self-reported response should be enriched in pathways implicated in antidepressant action and depression biology.
Here, we present the largest GWAS meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response.

We characterize its genetic architecture, test this hypothesis through pathway and drug-class enrichment analyses, and assess whether genetic liability to other psychiatric conditions is associated with reported outcome.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: Primary GWAS of self-reported SSRI response were conducted in three cohorts: All of Us Research Program (AoU; (13)), Genetic Links to Anxiety and Depression (GLAD; (14)), and UK Biobank (UKB; (15)) (Supplementary Note1).
text.formatted: Primary GWAS of self-reported SSRI response were conducted in three cohorts: All of Us Research Program (AoU; <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>), Genetic Links to Anxiety and Depression (GLAD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>), and UK Biobank (UKB; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>) (Supplementary Note1).

text.text: Binary SSRI response was derived from a retrospective, self-reported effectiveness question answered for each SSRI taken.
SSRIs included citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine and sertraline in all cohorts, plus escitalopram and fluvoxamine in GLAD.
For participants rating multiple SSRIs, majority positive ratings were classified as response and majority negative ratings as non-response.
Conflicting ratings (e.g., one positive and one negative) were excluded.

Analyses were limited to participants with lifetime MDD, defined by self-reported diagnoses (GLAD) or DSM-5 criteria applied to Composite International Diagnostic Interview -Short Form (CIDI-SF; AoU and UKB) (16).
text.formatted: Analyses were limited to participants with lifetime MDD, defined by self-reported diagnoses (GLAD) or DSM-5 criteria applied to Composite International Diagnostic Interview -Short Form (CIDI-SF; AoU and UKB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Participants reporting bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or psychosis were excluded.
Analyses were restricted to participants genetically similar to European-. ancestry reference individuals (EUR-like) due to small sample sizes in other ancestry groups (Supplementary TableS2).
In each cohort, GWAS was conducted using REGENIE (17), following sample-and variant-level quality control (Supplementary Note1).

Logistic regression tested associations between SSRI response and sequenced genotypes (AoU, UKB) or imputed dosages (GLAD) of common variants (MAF >0.01, INFO >0.7 in GLAD), adjusting for age at recruitment, genetic sex, the first six genetic principal components (PCs), and cohort-specific technical factors.

text.text: REGENIE's approximate Firth correction was applied at p-values <0.01.
text.formatted: REGENIE's approximate Firth correction was applied at p-values <0.01.

text.text: In addition to the primary GWAS (AoU, GLAD and UKB), summary statistics of self-reported SSRI response were obtained from published GWAS in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study [AGDS; (18)], Estonian Biobank [EstBB; (19)], and 23andMe Research Institute [23andMe; (20, 21)], as previously described (8) (Supplementary Note2).
text.formatted: In addition to the primary GWAS (AoU, GLAD and UKB), summary statistics of self-reported SSRI response were obtained from published GWAS in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study [AGDS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref>], Estonian Biobank [EstBB; <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>], and 23andMe Research Institute [23andMe; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>], as previously described (8) (Supplementary Note2).

text.text: Quality-controlled summary statistics were harmonized and meta-analyzed using an inversevariance-weighted fixed-effect (FE) model in bcftools v1.22 (22) with score plugins +munge, +liftover and +metal ((23); https://github.com/freeseek/score#run-meta-analysis), using the --overlap option to correct for sample overlap.

text.text: As a sensitivity analysis, Han and Eskin's modified random-effects (RE2) meta-analysis was implemented using METASOFT ((24); https://hanlab-snu.github.io/METASOFT/).

text.text: SNP-level heterogeneity between cohorts was assessed using I² and Cochran's Q statistics for SNPs in ≥3 cohorts (Supplementary Note3, Note4).
Genome-wide and suggestive significance were defined as p <5×10⁻⁸ and p <5×10⁻⁶, respectively.
text.formatted: Genome-wide and suggestive significance were defined as p <5×10⁻⁸ and p <5×10⁻⁶, respectively.

text.text: Independent genomic loci were defined in FUMA SNP2GENE (v1.8.2) (25) at the suggestive threshold (p <5×10⁻⁶), using the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 European reference panel (1KGP3 EUR), and SNPs within these loci were positionally mapped to protein-coding genes (Ensembl v102).

text.text: MAGMA (v1.08) (26) was used for gene-based association analyses (20,068 proteincoding genes), competitive gene-set analysis (17,012 MSigDB gene sets and GO terms) and tissue-expression analysis (54 specific and 30 general GTEx v8 tissues), with Bonferroni correction within each analysis.

text.text: Positionally mapped genes were characterized using GENE2FUNC.
Analyses were repeated on RE2 summary statistics (Supplementary Note5).

Meta-analytic SNP-based heritability (SNP-h²) was estimated using LD score regression (LDSC; (27)) and converted to the liability scale (28), assuming population prevalence equals sample prevalence (0.726).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic SNP-based heritability (SNP-h²) was estimated using LD score regression (LDSC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(27)</ref>) and converted to the liability scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(28)</ref>, assuming population prevalence equals sample prevalence (0.726).

text.text: Genetic correlations (rg) with 17 traits, spanning psychiatric conditions, personality, antidepressant response, BMI and educational attainment, were estimated using bivariate LDSC (Supplementary Note5, Supplementary TableS3).
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q < 0.05) was applied across with significant SNP-h² and a successfully estimated rg (Supplementary Note5 and Table S3).
text.formatted: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (q < 0.05) was applied across with significant SNP-h² and a successfully estimated rg (Supplementary Note5 and Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: Polygenic scores (PGS) were calculated with SBayesRC in GenoPred (v2.3.3) (29), using GCTB LD matrices from EUR-like UKB participants and restricted to HapMap3 SNPs (30) (31) (32); Supplementary Note5).
text.formatted: Polygenic scores (PGS) were calculated with SBayesRC in GenoPred (v2.3.3) (29), using GCTB LD matrices from EUR-like UKB participants and restricted to HapMap3 SNPs <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(30)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(31)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(32)</ref>; Supplementary Note5).

text.text: To evaluate the predictive performance of a self-reported SSRIresponse PGS, we constructed leave-one-out (LOO) PGS, excluding each target cohort (AGDS, AoU, GLAD) from the meta-analysis in turn.
Associations were tested using logistic regression . in unrelated participants, adjusting for age, sex and the first six PCs (AoU, GLAD) or sex and the first ten PCs (AGDS).
Variance explained was calculated as the incremental Nagelkerke's R² over a covariates-only model and converted to the liability scale (33), assuming a population prevalence of 0.726.
text.formatted: Variance explained was calculated as the incremental Nagelkerke's R² over a covariates-only model and converted to the liability scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(33)</ref>, assuming a population prevalence of 0.726.

text.text: Cohort-specific odds ratios (per SD of the PGS) were combined using fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis (metafor in R; (34)), with heterogeneity assessed using Cochran's Q and I².
text.formatted: Cohort-specific odds ratios (per SD of the PGS) were combined using fixed-effect inverse-variance meta-analysis (metafor in R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(34)</ref>), with heterogeneity assessed using Cochran's Q and I².

text.text: To examine shared genetic architecture, PGS for the traits in the genetic correlation analysis (Supplementary TableS3) were tested in AoU and GLAD (individual-level data access), using the same models, and meta-analyzed as above.
Each of the 17 PGS other than depression was tested unadjusted and adjusted for the depression PGS (35 tests), with FDR correction applied jointly given the correlation among PGS and models.
To identify which components of educational attainment (EA) drive its association, its cognitive (Cog) and non-cognitive (NonCog) components (35) were also tested.
To extend the FUMA gene-set analysis to all current KEGG pathways, we ran gene-set analyses in MAGMA (v1.10) (26) using the current KEGG release.

We tested gene-set enrichment in four pre-specified serotonin-related KEGG pathways (serotonergic synapse, neuroactive ligand signaling, tryptophan metabolism, and folate biosynthesis) (36, 37), and all 369 KEGG pathways.
text.formatted: We tested gene-set enrichment in four pre-specified serotonin-related KEGG pathways (serotonergic synapse, neuroactive ligand signaling, tryptophan metabolism, and folate biosynthesis) <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">37)</ref>, and all 369 KEGG pathways.

text.text: FDR correction was applied separately to each set, and gene-level p-values were examined for enriched pathways to identify signal drivers.

To test whether self-reported SSRI response is associated with genetically predicted gene expression or protein abundance, we performed transcriptome-and proteome-wide association analyses (TWAS and PWAS) using FUSION (38) and summary-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) (39), with brain and blood expression and protein quantitative trait locus (eQTL, pQTL) panels.
text.formatted: To test whether self-reported SSRI response is associated with genetically predicted gene expression or protein abundance, we performed transcriptome-and proteome-wide association analyses (TWAS and PWAS) using FUSION <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(38)</ref> and summary-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(39)</ref>, with brain and blood expression and protein quantitative trait locus (eQTL, pQTL) panels.

text.text: FDR correction was applied across panels within each method, separately for TWAS and PWAS.
Genes were prioritized as convergent candidates if they reached p <0.01 in the MAGMA genebased analysis, and in at least one brain panel for both TWAS and PWAS (Supplementary Note5).
text.formatted: Genes were prioritized as convergent candidates if they reached p <0.01 in the MAGMA genebased analysis, and in at least one brain panel for both TWAS and PWAS (Supplementary Note5).

text.text: These thresholds were used for prioritization, not as tests of significance.

To aid clinical interpretation, we tested whether gene-level associations were enriched for known drug targets using MAGMA (26) and TWAS-based Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (TWAS-GSEA; (40)), with drug-gene interactions from DrugTargetor (41).
text.formatted: To aid clinical interpretation, we tested whether gene-level associations were enriched for known drug targets using MAGMA <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(26)</ref> and TWAS-based Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (TWAS-GSEA; (40)), with drug-gene interactions from DrugTargetor <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(41)</ref>.

text.text: TWAS-GSEA is directional, testing whether a drug's predicted effect on expression aligns with or opposes the expression profile associated with response.
Drug-level results were FDR-corrected.

At the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) class level, for classes with at least five drugs, signed TWAS-GSEA statistics within each class were compared with those of all other drugs (twosided Wilcoxon rank-sum test; FDR-corrected across classes).
As drugs within a class often share targets, class-level results should be interpreted cautiously.

In the largest GWAS meta-analysis restricted to self-reported SSRI response, we found modest but significant SNP-based heritability (3.1%), with diagnostics indicating a polygenic signal rather than artefact.
However, no locus reached genome-wide significance in the primary fixed-effect analysis, and gene-based analysis was similarly null, with TIAM1 the strongest subthreshold signal.
At the current sample size and heritability, this GWAS appears underpowered for common-variant discovery; larger samples or more precise phenotyping will be needed.

Our work differs from a recent GWAS by Koch et al. (8) in that we used a single, consistently ascertained phenotype (self-reported response), restricted analyses to SSRIs and, where possible, to individuals with lifetime MDD, and added a new cohort, All of Us.

In our Han-Eskin random-effects sensitivity analysis, one locus (rs4884091) reached genomewide significance, driven by 23andMe2020.
This locus did not overlap Koch et al.'s genomewide significant locus but corresponded to their strongest self-report-restricted signal, which fell just below significance in their full analysis.
This likely reflects the same 23andMe-derived association, reported by Li et al. (20), resurfacing in each analysis rather than three independent findings.

text.text: In mouse models of chronic pain, Tiam1 . stabilizes synaptic N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), driving structural plasticity associated with ACC hyperactivity and depressive-like behavior, which low-dose ketamine reverses by blocking this pathway (44).

text.text: This places TIAM1 in a plausibly relevant glutamatergic pathway, though the evidence concerns ketamine, not SSRIs, and the finding warrants replication.
SSRIs block serotonin reuptake within hours, yet clinical improvement typically takes weeks, suggesting additional mechanisms, such as neuroplastic adaptation, are required for response (45).

text.text: We found no enrichment for serotonergic pathway genes, although this null may reflect limited power in small gene sets.

Instead, the FDR-significant KEGG nicotine addiction pathway was driven by GABA-A receptor and transporter genes, the glutamate transporter gene SLC17A6, and an AMPA receptor gene (GRIA4), with no contribution from nicotinic receptor genes, suggesting GABAergic and glutamatergic rather than nicotine-specific biology.
Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics, driven largely by anesthetics rather than ketamine, likewise points to GABA-A modulation.
GABAergic deficits are well documented in MDD (46, 47), glutamatergic and NMDA receptor dysfunction is implicated in MDD neuroimaging (48), and SSRIs also influence GABAergic neurotransmission (49).

text.text: SLC17A6 showed sub-threshold evidence across gene-level, pathway, transcriptome and proteome analyses, and TIAM1's role in synaptic plasticity offers a further route to downstream circuit change.
As these pathways are not SSRI-specific and power may differ across gene sets, we interpret them cautiously.

Self-reported response, unconstrained by a fixed assessment window, may capture delayed adaptation, plausibly contributing to the higher rates of self-reported benefit and the non-serotonergic signals observed here.

In TWAS-GSEA, where direction was interpretable, citalopram, fluoxetine and sertraline showed nominal expression effects opposing the responder-associated profile, as did antipsychotics and corticosteroids (FDR-significant), whereas dopamine-enhancing agents aligned with it.
Two non-exclusive interpretations are possible.

Opposition suggests a drug counteracting an expression state that predisposes to poorer outcomes, so responders are those whose baseline profile is most amenable to reversal along that drug's axis of action.
Alignment suggests a drug shifting expression towards a profile responders already carry, so reproducing rather than reversing it.

Both could operate for different drug classes, and the present data cannot distinguish them; as the responder profile reflects genetically predicted expression rather than measured pre-and post-treatment expression, these results are hypothesis-generating.

The leave-one-out self-reported SSRI-response PGS was significantly associated with selfreported response, indicating the GWAS captures genuine common-variant signal despite insufficient power for locus discovery, as in other psychiatric traits where SNP-based heritability is detectable well before genome-wide significant loci emerge (50, 51).

text.text: Genetic liability to most psychiatric disorders was associated with poorer self-reported response, extending beyond shared liability to depression for ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction, but not for anxiety and schizophrenia.
The persistent ADHD association is consistent with prior work linking ADHD PGS to treatment-resistant depression (52).

text.text: Most associations were supported by genetic correlations; those significant only in PGS analyses (autism, addiction and schizophrenia) likely reflect the lower power of rg estimation.

These associations may reflect biological non-response in individuals with greater comorbid psychiatric burden, behavioral factors linked to these traits, or misdiagnosis, where depression secondary to an unrecognized condition such as ADHD is treated as MDD, so that apparent non-response.
reflects an unaddressed diagnosis rather than pharmacological failure (53).

text.text: Although these PGS, like the SSRI-response PGS, explain too little variance to guide individual treatment, if replicated, polygenic loading for comorbid traits could help identify patients who warrant closer monitoring or diagnostic reassessment.

Among personality traits, only agreeableness remained associated with better response after adjustment for depression PGS, whereas the neuroticism association largely reflected shared liability to depression.

Agreeableness has been linked to stronger therapeutic alliance and modestly better outcomes in psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy (54), but also to an approval-oriented, socially desirable self-presentation (55), which may inflate self-reported treatment benefit.

text.text: EA PGS was among the strongest and most robust predictors of better self-reported response.

It captures genetic influences on cognitive ability, socioeconomic status and health-related behaviors (56,57), and can be decomposed into a cognitive (Cog) component, shared with cognitive performance, and a non-cognitive (NonCog) component, linked to personality, decision-making and lower health-risk behavior (35).

text.text: Both components were associated with better response, with similar effect sizes, independent of depression PGS.
As both are similarly genetically correlated with income (35), socioeconomic factors are a plausible shared contributor.

text.text: This is consistent with evidence that EA and cognitive performance PGS distinguish treatment-resistant from treatment-responsive depression in electronic health records (58).

text.text: In conclusion, self-reported SSRI response captures genuine genetic signal relevant to antidepressant response, although current samples remain underpowered for commonvariant discovery.

Our findings implicate GABAergic and glutamatergic mechanisms alongside broader psychiatric burden: higher genetic liability for ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction was associated with poorer self-reported response independent of depression liability, and genetic . propensity for higher educational attainment with better response.
As a patient-centered and scalable phenotype, self-report offers a practical route to the larger samples this trait requires.

text.text: Several pathways could link these components to response.
Antidepressant treatment requires patients to persist through early side effects and delayed benefit, and to recognize when to seek review.
Cognitive ability may support such persistence, consistent with links . between health literacy and adherence(59).
text.formatted: Cognitive ability may support such persistence, consistent with links . between health literacy and adherence<ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(59)</ref>.

text.text: Non-cognitive traits such as persistence, future orientation and engagement with healthcare may similarly support adherence and follow-up, while socioeconomic advantage, captured by both components, may improve access to and continuity of care.
These pathways were not testable here, and the associations may also reflect how response is reported.This study has several limitations.

Our phenotype relies on cross-sectional, retrospective selfreport, which is subject to recall and reporting bias and may capture improvements in wellbeing not specific to antidepressant pharmacology, such as changing life circumstances, placebo response or non-specific therapeutic benefit.
Question wording and response options differed across cohorts, which may have reduced power for an already low-heritability trait.
Genetic contributions to response may also change over the lifespan, warranting longitudinal data.

Available data remains overwhelmingly of European ancestry, reflecting the underrepresentation of non-European populations in genetic and mental health research, compounded by underrepresentation in follow-up questionnaires from which response phenotypes were derived.

Addressing these gaps will require larger, multi-ancestry samples; functional follow-up of the GABAergic and glutamatergic signals, particularly SLC17A6; and work disentangling general psychiatric liability from treatment-response-specific genetics.
